trust.lead: What Foundry does, where, what it keeps, and the one limit you should know about.

where.title: What runs where
where.body: Everything runs on this computer. The page listens on this computer only, and nothing listens on your network. Your automations and records are in this folder, private to your user:

leaves.title: What leaves this computer
leaves.body: Foundry itself sends one thing: when you press Check and save on an AI key, one request to that provider with the key, and only if Allowed AI includes that provider. Nothing else: e-mails are drafts you send, chat messages are drafts you paste. If you use Foundry through a coding agent, what Foundry tells the agent (counts, step names, test results on pretend data) goes to that agent's AI provider under your agreement with them; the recipients and text of a real list are shown only in this page. AI builders: Mercury (Inception) only if Allowed AI says so and a key is saved; Claude Haiku (Anthropic) only if Foundry is started with it and Allowed AI says so. Neither is on by default.

keys.title: Keys
keys.body: AI keys go into your computer's keychain. Foundry never writes them to a file, a log or the AI's view. If your computer has no keychain Foundry can use, it doesn't save the key. A keychain keeps the key from other users of this computer, not from programs running as you: on a Mac, Foundry saves it in a way that lets any program running as you read it back through the security command without asking you (from Apple's documentation; not tried on a Mac), and on Linux any program running as you can read it while your keyring is unlocked. {claim:C10}

approve.title: Who can approve
approve.body: You decide: with a click on this page, a typed yes in your own terminal, or, when Foundry finds nothing that could answer it for you, the dialog Claude Code shows you. Foundry gives your agent no tool that approves. {claim:C02}
approve.whyOnce: Why Foundry asks once, about the whole list, rather than about each e-mail: {claim:C11}

limit.title: The honest limit
limit.body: A coding agent that can run commands as you on this computer could do what you can do, including approve. Foundry's link key and checks keep out other web pages and other users, not that agent.
limit.closes: What could close this gap: Foundry running as a separate user, approvals on a second device, or the hosted Team plan. These are options we have written down; none of them is built or scheduled.

pilot.title: For IT: the pilot we suggest
items: Practice-only mode for every Foundry folder on the pilot machines, set by IT in /etc/foundry/policy.json (owned by root): the page then shows it as set by your organisation, with no off switch in the page. A user who runs a modified copy of Foundry can still get around it: it is a control for honest machines, not a sandbox
No AI, or only the provider you approve
Linux developer machines (macOS and Windows are untested)
Allowlist the exact command below, not the name, with allowManagedMcpServersOnly on (otherwise a user can add servers of their own), and with Foundry installed where only root can change it
In Claude Code's managed settings, allowManagedHooksOnly on, so only hooks your organisation sets can answer Foundry's dialog (recommended wherever plugins are used)
Check a machine at any time: node app/cli.mjs doctor --json

allowlist.title: Allowlist entry (exact)
allowlist.body: For Claude Code's managed settings: allow Foundry's exact command, every argument in order, generated on this computer, and turn on allowManagedMcpServersOnly so this list is the only one.
allowlist.mcpLead: Or, if your organisation sets every server itself, a managed-mcp entry:
allowlist.note: Claude Code matches every argument in order; a server name is not a security control (code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp, read 2026-10-21). Without allowManagedMcpServersOnly, allowlists from every settings scope merge, so a user can add servers of their own, a copy of Foundry included: a soft allowlist (same page). This entry decides which command may start. It does not check Foundry's files, which the user can edit, or variables such as NODE_OPTIONS that change what node loads: install Foundry in a folder only root can change, and allowlist that path. The paths are this computer's.

hooks.title: Dialogs a hook can answer
hooks.body: A hook in Claude Code's settings, or in a plugin, skill or subagent, can answer Foundry's dialog without showing it to you, or change your answer. So Foundry uses that dialog only when it can look for such hooks and finds none. The line from the Connect page includes --consent, which lets Foundry read Claude Code's settings, plugins, skills and subagents on this computer, only to look for those hooks, and it looks again each time it asks. It asks you in this page instead if it finds one, if your organisation manages Claude Code, if Claude Code was started in a way that can bring hooks Foundry can't see, or if your agent isn't Claude Code. A hook Foundry can't see could still answer, so a yes in the dialog is recorded as the weaker way. Foundry can't see hooks that reach Claude Code from settings your organisation sends over the network or through a device-management profile, or from a plugin or skill kept outside the folders it reads. If you use plugins, ask IT to turn on allowManagedHooksOnly in Claude Code's managed settings: then only hooks your organisation sets can run.

data.title: What Foundry keeps, and how to delete it
data.body: Only the columns a card needs from the lists you give, the drafts it made, run records and your decisions, all in your Foundry folder, which Foundry makes private to your user each time it starts (Settings says so if it can't, for example when the folder is your home folder). Replaced lists are kept until you delete them (Settings: Delete my lists). Outside that folder: an AI key in your keychain, if you saved one; this tab's key in the browser tab; and any file you download. Foundry doesn't encrypt anything itself: if your computer's disk is encrypted, that protects these files while it is off; if it isn't, nothing does. To remove everything, delete the Foundry folder.

remove.title: Removing Foundry
remove.body: Remove it from Claude Code with: claude mcp remove foundry (other agents: delete the foundry entry from their settings). Remove a saved AI key in Settings, AI keys. Then delete the Foundry folder. There is no background service, no auto-update and no schedule: stopping Foundry stops it.

glossary.lead: The site uses everyday words. Developers and IT will see the precise ones.
rows: A fixed list of steps Foundry runs for you.
Running a version with made-up data and a pretend inbox. Nothing real is sent.
A local file standing in for e-mail or a spreadsheet during a test.
Every change makes a new version with its own fingerprint. A yes covers one version only.
A version that is tested but not turned on yet.

The planned paid part, for when someone else's yes has to count as theirs. It isn't available yet.
Whether an AI was used, and for what.

E-mails Foundry writes on this computer for you to send.

help.lead: Short answers. Each one has a next step.
qa: Do I need an account or a key?
No. Foundry runs on this computer with no account and no AI key.
I closed the page. How do I get back?
While Foundry is running, your bookmark of its page opens it. If the page asks for its link, run the open command shown there in a terminal on this computer.
Will it send anything without asking me?
No e-mail, ever: it makes drafts you send yourself, and it shows you every one in full before it makes them. The only thing it sends itself is a check of an AI key you choose to save.
Can it run by itself every week?
Not yet. You press Run, or add a calendar reminder to do it.
What if my list looks different from the pretend one?
Drop your own list: Foundry asks which column is which, and asks anything it can't tell.
My coding agent wants to approve. Can it?
Not through Foundry's tools. It can draft and test; you decide, in its dialog or in this page. An agent that can run any command as you could still approve as you.
Every error says what happened, what wasn't done, and what to do next. Runs keep a record you can download.
My IT team asked what this is.
Give them the one-page brief. It is written on this computer and sent nowhere.

org.rulesTitle: Rules Foundry checks when you make an automation
org.rulesLead: A rule is one sentence Foundry can check, with an owner and a layer. You confirm it with examples, and the examples become its tests.
org.noRulesYet: No rules yet. Make one from a row above.
org.ownedBy: Written down by you for {owner}. {owner} has not confirmed it.
org.confirmed: Confirmed. These cases are now the rule's tests.
org.doesNotCover: What this rule does not cover
org.examplesBecomeTests: Saving a new version re-checks every confirmed case. If a change would flip one, Foundry asks you first.
org.whereTitle: Where it runs and what it may touch
org.changeBody: Who can change these rules: you. Each change is a new version, saved by you and recorded as self-approved.
org.editingLead: Nothing changes until you save a new version.
org.flipTitle: This change would change a confirmed answer
org.confirmFlip: Confirm the new answer for case {n} ({now})
org.chainOk: History checked: {n} versions, each linked to the one before.
org.chainBad: The history could not be checked.
org.remindersPlanned: Planned: a reminder after a day. Today nothing reminds anyone.
org.requesterPlanned: Planned: whoever asked for it can't approve it. Not checked yet.
org.whenBroken: When an automation is made, Foundry refuses settings that break this rule.
org.moreTitle: More: where it runs, and changing these rules
